Its main contributors were the German Jesuit theologians Gustav Gundlach and Oswald von Nell-Breuning, the latter through the Königswinter Circle. Heinrich Pesch was a further influence. The first part reviews and applauds Leo XIII's letter and credits the Church with helping to form a new social conscience.

The encyclical holds that private property is essential to individual development and freedom, but that it has a social function and loses its moral value if it is not subordinated to the common good. Governments may therefore pursue redistribution and, in extreme cases, expropriate. A fair wage rests on three things: the needs of the worker and his family, the condition of the enterprise and the state of the whole economy.

Pius XI called for solidarity between employers and employees in place of class conflict, and criticised anonymous international finance for squeezing small and medium-sized firms. He condemned communism and held that socialism, even in a moderate form, cannot be reconciled with Catholic teaching. He also upheld a family wage so that mothers need not work outside the home.

Ramsay MacDonald asked Cardinal Bourne how the letter's statements on socialism applied to Catholics, and the cardinal replied that nothing in it should deter them from joining the British Labour Party. Franklin D. Roosevelt praised the encyclical and quoted it extensively, especially on the evils of concentrated economic power. Portugal under the Estado Novo and Austria under the Fatherland Front both welcomed it and tried to put elements of it into practice. It has since been an inspiration to distributist thought, which seeks greater solidarity and subsidiarity than capitalism offers.
quakers: Members of the Religious Society of Friends call one another Friends, after John 15:14. The name Quakers was first used by others, because George Fox told a judge to quake before the authority of God and because critics said that they shook or trembled while preaching. The movement arose in mid-17th-century England among dissenting Protestant groups that broke with the Church of England, many of which emerged during and after the English Civil War. In 1647 Fox claimed to have received a revelation that there is one, Christ Jesus, who can speak to a person's condition. He became convinced that a direct experience of Christ was possible without ordained clergy, and travelled through England, the Netherlands and Barbados preaching it.

The early preachers, above all the group known as the Valiant Sixty, travelled in Britain and overseas, and some were women. Quaker women published at least 220 texts in the 17th century, and Margaret Fell helped to define the movement. Persecution reached North America in July 1656, when Mary Fisher and Ann Austin began preaching in Boston; they were imprisoned for five weeks and banished by the Massachusetts Bay Colony. By 1700 the boisterous behaviour of the first years was no longer supported, and in the 18th century Quakers turned inward and converted fewer people.

Quakers were granted exemption from military service in Great Britain in 1757. In the early 1700s disquiet about slavery arose among Friends, many of whom in colonial America owned slaves, and the testimonies of Benjamin Lay, Anthony Benezet and John Woolman led to an abolition movement. Splits followed in America during the Revolutionary War and in the 19th century, and British Friends began missions in India in 1866.

Friends reject priests, hold to the priesthood of all believers and mostly believe in continuing revelation. Traditionally they wore plain dress, avoided alcohol, refused to swear oaths or take part in war, and used a plain calendar of numbered days and months. In unprogrammed worship there is no plan: Friends gather in expectant waiting, and anyone moved to speak stands and does so, with silence after each message. Others hold programmed worship with hymns, Bible readings and a pastor.

Decisions are taken at a meeting for worship for church business, in which members seek God's will. Quaker families founded the firms of Barclays, Lloyds, Clarks, Cadbury, Rowntree and Fry. In 1947 the British Friends Service Council and the American Friends Service Committee were awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.
quanah-parker: His mother, Cynthia Ann Parker, had been captured by Comanches in 1836 during the raid on Fort Parker near present-day Groesbeck, Texas, adopted into the Nokoni band and married to the Kwahadi warrior chief Peta Nocona. Quanah was their first child, born, by his own account, on Elk Creek below the Wichita Mountains. In December 1860 his mother and infant sister Topʉ̠sana were taken during the Pease River Massacre and returned against her will to her family. His name, Kwana, means a smell or odour, and he kept it in tribute to her.

After his father's death, around 1864, the Nokoni chief Horseback took Quanah and his brother Pecos under his wing and taught them the ways of a Comanche warrior. In October 1867 Quanah attended the treaty negotiations at Medicine Lodge, Kansas, as an observer and refused to sign.

In 1873 he and Kwihnai Tosaabitʉ, who claimed to be a medicine man, recruited warriors for raids into Texas. On 27 June 1874 a war party of about 250, mostly Comanches and Cheyennes, attacked the hide hunters' trading post at Adobe Walls; Sharps rifles drove them back and Quanah was wounded. The attack led to the Red River War, in which Colonel Ranald Mackenzie razed the Comanche village at Palo Duro Canyon on 28 September 1874 and killed nearly 1,500 horses. Short of food, the Kwahadi came into Fort Sill in late May and early June 1875.

The federal government appointed him principal chief of the whole Comanche Nation, though the tribe never elected him. Having first opposed grazing leases, he worked with cattlemen such as Charles Goodnight and Samuel Burk Burnett, and in 1884 his efforts won the tribes their first grass payments. He built herds of his own and the Star House at Cache, Oklahoma. He hunted wolves with President Theodore Roosevelt in 1905 and pressed him, in vain, to keep 400,000 acres from sale to homesteaders.

He is credited as one of the first important leaders of the Native American Church, holding peyote to be a sacrament given to Indian peoples. He had eight wives and twenty-five children. He died at the Star House on 23 February 1911; his remains were moved to Fort Sill Post Cemetery in 1957. The critic Paul Chaat Smith called the question of whether he was a sellout or a patriot the basic Comanche political question.
quang-binh-province: Quảng Bình lies on the narrow coast of north-central Vietnam, with Hà Tĩnh to the north, Quảng Trị to the south, Laos to the west and the sea to the east. At its narrowest the province is only 40 kilometres from the sea to the Laotian border. Hills and mountains cover 85 per cent of it, and the Annamite Range forms the border with Laos, its highest peak, Phi Co Pi, rising to 2,017 metres. A belt of sand dunes along the coast acts as a natural dam against the tides. Most of its rivers rise in the Truong Son Range and flow to the sea, among them the Gianh and the Nhật Lệ.

Excavations show that people lived in the area in the Stone Age. In 1926 the French archaeologist Madeleine Colani excavated caves in the western mountains and assigned the finds to the Hòa Bình culture, with a radiocarbon date of 10,509 years ago, plus or minus 950. Some pottery from the Đông Sơn culture was also found. Under the Hùng kings the area belonged to the Việt Thường group.

King Chế Củ of Champa adopted a hostile policy toward the Vietnamese, and in 1068 he provoked a conflict. In February 1069 the fleet of King Lý Thánh Tông of Đại Việt scattered the Cham forces at the mouth of the Nhật Lệ River and took the Cham capital, Vijaya. Chế Củ was captured and secured his release only by ceding three districts, Bố Chính, Địa-ly and Ma-Linh, corresponding to present-day Quảng Bình and northern Quảng Trị. In 1469 the area became the Tân Bình prefecture, and in 1604 it was named Quảng Bình.

In the 17th century, during the Trịnh-Nguyễn war, the Gianh River became the border between Đàng Trong in the south and Đàng Ngoài in the north, and Đồng Hới was built as a fortress to protect the Nguyễn lords' territory. Quảng Bình became an important front. Under French rule it belonged to Annam. After the division of Vietnam in 1954 it was the southernmost province of North Vietnam, and during the Vietnam War it was the most heavily bombed province, by U.S. B-52s. In 1976 it was merged with Quảng Trị and Thừa Thiên into Bình Trị Thiên, and in 1990 the three were separated again.

On 12 June 2025 Quảng Bình was dissolved and merged with Quảng Trị province. Its capital was Đồng Hới. The Phong Nha-Kẻ Bàng National Park, listed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 2003, protects a karst region with some 300 caves and grottoes, including the longest underground river, and Sơn Đoòng Cave is open only to limited guided tours.
quang-trung: Nguyễn Huệ was born in 1753 in Tây Sơn village, in Quy Nhơn Province, then in the south of the country. His ancestors were peasants from Nghệ An, and his birth name was Hồ Thơm. His father had eight children, three of whom took part in the Tây Sơn Rebellion: Nguyễn Nhạc, Nguyễn Lữ and Huệ.

After two centuries of rule, the Nguyễn lords had weakened, and after the death of Lord Nguyễn Phúc Khoát the official Trương Phúc Loan took control of the government. The brothers gathered an army and revolted, and quickly occupied the central part of the Nguyễn territory from Quy Nhơn to Bình Thuận. In 1776 Nhạc proclaimed himself King of Tây Sơn and gave Huệ the title Phụ Chính. In 1777 Huệ and Lữ captured Saigon and destroyed the Nguyễn army, killing most of the family except Nguyễn Ánh.

In 1786 an army under Huệ marched north, took Phú Xuân and then Thăng Long. Lê Hiển Tông welcomed him, gave him the title of supreme commander and a daughter, Lê Ngọc Hân, in marriage. When Nhạc proclaimed himself Central Emperor, the brothers fell into civil war, which ended with a boundary agreed at Bến Bản.

In late 1788 two Chinese armies invaded to restore the Lê emperor Lê Chiêu Thống, at the wish of the Qianlong Emperor. Huệ then sought to restore the tributary relationship, writing as Nguyễn Quang Bình, and in 1789 Qianlong made him King of Annam, on condition that he lead a delegation to Beijing; Chinese and Vietnamese sources agree that he sent an imposter. He nevertheless regarded himself as emperor of Đại Việt. On the advice of Nguyễn Thiếp he began a new capital at Phượng Hoàng Trung Đô in Nghệ An and renamed Thăng Long Bắc Thành.

Quang Trung fell ill suddenly and died on 16 September 1792, at about 40. The official records do not name the illness, and historians think a stroke possible. On his deathbed he called his heir Nguyễn Quang Toản a clever boy but too young. Toản did not continue his policies, and Nguyễn Ánh overthrew the Tây Sơn in 1802, razing the tombs of Nhạc and Huệ.

Quang Trung came to be regarded as a national saviour and one of Vietnam's most popular figures; most cities have named major streets after him, and a museum in his hometown shows documents and artifacts of the Tây Sơn.
quantum-mechanics: Quantum mechanics arose gradually from attempts to explain observations that classical physics could not account for. Scientific inquiry into the wave nature of light began in the 17th and 18th centuries, when Robert Hooke, Christiaan Huygens and Leonhard Euler proposed a wave theory of light, and in 1803 Thomas Young described the double-slit experiment, which played a major role in the general acceptance of that theory. Max Planck's solution to the black-body radiation problem and the correspondence between energy and frequency in Albert Einstein's paper on the photoelectric effect are the best-known early steps. These attempts, now called the old quantum theory, led in the mid-1920s to the full theory, developed by Niels Bohr, Erwin Schrödinger, Werner Heisenberg, Max Born, Paul Dirac and others.

The theory describes matter and light at and below the scale of atoms, where classical physics is insufficient. Quantum systems have bound states quantized to discrete values of energy, momentum and angular momentum, whereas classical systems can take them continuously. Measurements show characteristics of both particles and waves, and the uncertainty principle sets limits on how accurately the value of a physical quantity can be predicted before it is measured. In one formalism the wave function gives probability amplitudes for what measurements of a particle's energy, momentum and other properties may yield, and its change in time is described by the Schrödinger equation.

Several mathematically equivalent formulations exist. Dirac's transformation theory unifies the two earliest, Heisenberg's matrix mechanics and Schrödinger's wave mechanics, and Richard Feynman's path integral formulation treats an amplitude as a sum over all possible paths between an initial and a final state. Classical mechanics can be derived from quantum mechanics as an approximation valid at ordinary scales.

Quantum mechanics has been verified experimentally to an extremely high degree of accuracy. Quantum electrodynamics, the first complete quantum field theory, agrees with experiment to within 1 part in 10 to the power 12 for the magnetic properties of an electron. Solid-state physics and materials science depend on it, and its applications include quantum chemistry, superconducting magnets, light-emitting diodes, the optical amplifier, the laser, the transistor and the microprocessor, and imaging such as magnetic resonance imaging and electron microscopy.

Its counter-intuitive results have provoked philosophical debate since the start, centred on probability, wavefunction collapse and the measurement problem. The views of Bohr, Heisenberg and others are grouped as the Copenhagen interpretation, which treats the probabilistic nature of the theory as final rather than temporary. Steven Weinberg judged that there is no entirely satisfactory interpretation. Its formalism and that of general relativity contradict each other, and reconciling them has been a major goal of physics since the 20th century.
quanzhen-school: According to traditional legend, Wang Chongyang met the immortals Zhongli Quan and Lü Dongbin in the summer of 1159, who taught him Daoist beliefs and secret rituals. On meeting one of them again in 1160 he received five written instructions, and he went to live in a grave he dug for himself on Zhongnan Mountain for three years, then four more in a hut he called the Complete Perfection Hut. Kunyu mountain in Shandong is held to be the school's birthplace.

Wang gathered seven disciples, later called the Seven Masters of Quanzhen, among them Tan Chuduan and Qiu Chuji, and in 1167 in Shandong Ma Yu and his wife Sun Bu'er. After Wang, Ma Yu led the school.

Quanzhen specialises in Neidan, the internal alchemy of the body, rather than Waidan, the ingestion of herbs and minerals, and like most Taoists its priests sought longevity, harmony with the Dao and balance of Yin and Yang. Wang held that Buddhism, Confucianism and Daoism were like the three legs of a tripod and had his followers study the Classic of Filial Piety and the Heart Sutra.

Its adepts are expected to keep celibacy and to meditate in a cell on alchemical poems until enlightenment; an ordination certificate of 1244 shows it took its precepts from a Tang dynasty text almost unchanged. According to Louis Komjathy its chief scriptures are the Daodejing, the Classic of Clarity and Stillness and the Yinfujing, followed by Wang's writings such as the Fifteen Discourses to Establish the Teachings.

The school became popular in Jin-ruled northern China, partly as a reaction against the privileged place of Jurchens in the civil service examinations, but it did not spread to the Southern Song. Qiu Chuji was on good terms with Genghis Khan, who put him in charge of religious affairs, and the school flourished long after its founder's death. Each of the seven masters founded a branch: Qiu Chuji's Longmen or Dragon Gate lineage remains one of the largest Daoist sects in China, and Sun Bu'er founded the Purity and Tranquility School.
quanzhou: Quanzhou lies on a strip of land between the estuaries of the Jin River and the Luoyang River, where they flow into Quanzhou Bay on the Taiwan Strait. Foreign traders knew it as Zaiton or Zayton, from the Arabic name meaning City of Olives, which is traditionally linked to its Chinese epithet, the Coral-tree City, after the coral trees said to have been planted around it by its 10th-century ruler Liu Congxiao.

Quanzhou proper was established under the Tang in 718, and Muslim traders reached it early. After the fall of the Min state, the Qingyuan Circuit, with Quanzhou as its capital, was de facto independent from 949 to 978 under Liu Congxiao, who promoted overseas trade. In the first century of the Northern Song it became the starting point of the Maritime Silk Road, eclipsing Guangzhou. A 1095 inscription records two convoys of twenty ships each arriving from the Southern Seas every year, and celadon made for export accounted for ninety percent of Fujian's ceramic production. A report of 1206 lists merchants from Arabia, Iran, India, Sumatra, Java, Korea and Japan, and Tamil merchants built Hindu temples there.

Under the Yuan, a superintendent of foreign trade was established in 1277. Marco Polo recorded a 10 percent duty on the port's commerce and described it as one of the two chief havens for commerce in the world; Ibn Battuta ranked it first among the world's ports. Kublai Khan's invasions of Japan and Java sailed mainly from it. From 1357 a revolt by the Persian garrison against anti-Muslim laws lasted a decade and was followed by massacres of foreign communities. Under the Ming, foreign commerce was discouraged; piracy forced the Superintendency of Trade to close in 1522, and silting of the harbour later hindered larger ships.

Quanzhou is a prefecture-level city with a population of 8,782,285 at the 2020 census. In 2021 Quanzhou: Emporium of the World in Song-Yuan China was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. The Qingjing Mosque, which dates from 1009, is now a museum, and the Kaiyuan Temple has two five-storey pagodas of the 13th century. About 6 million overseas Chinese, most in Southeast Asia, trace their ancestry to the Quanzhou area.
quba: Quba is the administrative centre of the Quba District of Azerbaijan. It lies on the north-eastern slopes of the Shahdag mountain, at an altitude of 600 metres, on the right bank of the Kudyal River, 168 km from Baku. The city grew from a riverside village called Gudial. The Quba region has a humid subtropical climate. The great majority of its people are Azerbaijanis, with Tats and Lezgians as minorities.

European geographers and ancient Arabic and Albanian sources mention the place. A castle built by the ruler Anushiravan in the 11th century was called Bade-Firuz Qubat. Arabic sources of the 12th century name it Cuba, a geographical dictionary of the 13th century has Kubba, and sources of the 16th century call it Dome.

In the mid-18th century Hussain Ali moved his residence from Khudat and became khan of Quba, raising fortress walls around the city. He tried to create a state separate from the other Caucasian khanates. The Quba Khanate grew stronger under his son Fatali Khan, who reigned from 1758 to 1789. Like the other Transcaucasian khanates it was occupied by Czarist Russia in the early 19th century and formally annexed to the Russian Empire under the agreement of 1813. Quba was included in the Derbent province in 1840 and in 1860 became part of the Kuba Uyezd of the Baku Governorate. Alexandre Dumas, the orientalist Berezin, the writer Bestuzhev-Marlinsky and the Norwegian Thor Heyerdahl are said to have visited it.

Quba has long been a centre of carpet weaving: the carpet Golu Chichi was woven there in 1712 and has been shown at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. In 2007 a mass grave was found of victims killed in 1918 during the events known as the March Days, and a memorial was opened on the site in 2013.

Quba's suburb of Qırmızı Qəsəbə, formerly Krasnaya Sloboda, meaning Red Town, is home to the largest community of Mountain Jews in Azerbaijan, one of the largest Jewish populations in the former Soviet Union. The city's red-brick Juma Mosque was erected in 1802, an octagonal building with a dome 16 m across. The Sakina-Khanum Mosque dates from 1854, and the Chuhur hamam is a bathhouse with a brick beehive dome, used until 1985. The bridge over the Kudyalchay, built in 1894 with 14 brick spans and a length of 275 m, is the only one of seven bridges once in the district to survive. Local cuisine reflects its multicultural history.
quchan: Quchan is the capital of Quchan County and its Central District in Razavi Khorasan province, in north-eastern Iran. It stands at an elevation of 1,149 metres, north of the Shah Jahan Mountains and south of the border with Turkmenistan. It is connected by road to Mashhad, 125 kilometres to the south-east, and to Turkmenistan, 100 kilometres to the north. The climate is cold semi-arid. Quchan has suffered many earthquakes. Most of its people are Kurdish, of the Zafaranlu tribe, who once spoke Kurdish and now speak Khorasani Turkish.

Local historical writing connects the area with the early Parthians. The city of Asak, near present-day Quchan, is said to be where the founder of the Parthian dynasty was crowned king, and the area is held to have been among the oldest Parthian centres. Some writers place an eternal fire there that continued into the Sasanian era. These accounts rest on traditions and speculation, and a thorough investigation of the sites has been called for.

Quchan was recognised as one of seven districts of Greater Khorasan when the first law of national division was approved in 1316, and in January 1915 it was one of the cities of the ninth province, with Mashhad as its capital. In 1895, after an earthquake the previous year, the present city was built 12 kilometres from it, with the help of Mohammad Nasser Khan Shoa al-Dowleh, head of the Zafranlu tribe, and Russian engineers. Under Reza Shah, Germans built a silo, a water source and the Atrak Bridge there. Nader Shah was assassinated at Quchan in Khorasan on 20 June 1747.

The 2016 census counted 101,604 people in the city. It has two industrial towns, and the Quchan University of Technology and a branch of the Islamic Azad University. The town is credited with 140 historical monuments, of which 32 are on the national list.
quedlinburg: Quedlinburg lies just north of the Harz mountains, mostly in the western part of the valley of the Bode, a river that flows from the Harz into the Saale. The town centre stands about 123 metres above sea level. Quedlinburg was the capital of its district until 2007, when the district was dissolved, and it has belonged to the state of Saxony-Anhalt since German reunification in 1990.

A settlement called Gross Orden stood on the eastern bank of the Bode by the early 9th century, and Quedlinburg was first mentioned as a town in 922, in a donation by King Henry the Fowler. According to legend, Franconian nobles offered Henry the German crown there in 919. After Henry's death in 936 his widow, Saint Matilda, founded a community of women on the castle hill, where daughters of the higher nobility were educated and whose main task was to pray for Henry and his successors.

In 973 an imperial assembly was held at the court, at which Mieszko, duke of the Polans, Boleslav, duke of Bohemia, and nobles from as far away as Byzantium and Bulgaria paid homage to Emperor Otto I. In 994 Otto III granted the town the rights of market, tax and coinage. Quedlinburg joined the Hanseatic League in 1426.

The abbey often disputed the town's independence, and in 1477 Abbess Hedwig expelled the forces of the Bishopric of Halberstadt, which had supported the town. The town then left the League and was protected by the Electorate of Saxony. Town and abbey became Lutheran in 1539. In 1697 Frederick Augustus I of Poland-Saxony sold his rights to the Elector Frederick III of Brandenburg for 240,000 thalers. After the abbey was secularised, Quedlinburg passed to Prussia. Its abbesses, who were free to marry, ruled the town until then; the last was the Swedish princess Sofia Albertina.

The old town, with about 2,000 half-timbered houses, is among the largest in Germany. The oldest, a timber-framed Ständerbau, dates from 1347. The castle hill, the collegiate church of St Servatius, a prime example of German Romanesque style, and the old town have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1994. The church's treasure, stolen by an American soldier, was returned to Quedlinburg in 1993. The poet Friedrich Gottlieb Klopstock was born in the town, which has more than 24,000 inhabitants.
queen-amina: Zazzau, around present-day Zaria in Kaduna State, was one of the seven original Hausa states, and before Amina's time it was already among the largest; it was also the main source of the enslaved people sold by Arab merchants in the markets of Kano and Katsina. Oral traditions collected by the anthropologist David E. Jones make her the daughter of a King Nikatau and Queen Bakwa Turunku, raised at her grandfather's court and taught political and military matters. Nikatau, however, appears in no early Hausa chronicle, and the king-lists compiled by E. J. Arnett name Bakwa Turunku as a male king.

In Jones's account she was named Magajiya, heir apparent, at 16, refused many suitors, and became a leading warrior in her brother's cavalry. Palace tradition calls her queen, while other traditions say she remained a princess.

Some traditions hold that she took the throne after the death of her brother Karama and spent 34 years at war with her neighbours. Blocked to the north by Kano and Katsina and to the east by the Jos Plateau, she campaigned south-east and south-west with an army said to number 20,000 foot soldiers and 1,000 cavalry, taking Bauchi and Yauri. The Chronicle of Abuja says the ruler of Nupe sent her 40 eunuchs and 10,000 kola nuts, which introduced kola to Hausaland. Sultan Muhammad Bello of Sokoto claimed that Katsina and Kano paid her tribute, a claim present-day historians dispute.

The 19th-century scholar Dan Tafa says she died at a place called Attaagar, probably Idah, south of the Niger-Benue confluence; other writers place her death at Vom in Jos. Dating her is difficult: the Kano Chronicle makes her a contemporary of Muhammad Dauda, who ruled from 1421 to 1438, some scholars place her in the early 16th century through her link to Bakwa Turunku, and the historian Abdullahi Smith dates her reign after 1576. The historian Michael Crowder observed that the influence of ruling-class Hausa women steadily declined after her. Her earthen walls, the ganuwar Amina, were built across the region until the British conquest of Zazzau in 1904, and a statue of her stands at the National Arts Theatre in Lagos.
queen-of-sheba: The Queen of Sheba, named Bilqis in Arabic and Makeda in Geʽez, is first mentioned in the Hebrew Bible, where her name is not given. She came to Jerusalem with a very great retinue, with camels bearing spices, very much gold and precious stones. Her story has been greatly elaborated in Judaism, Ethiopian Christianity and Islam. Modern historians and archaeologists place Sheba among the South Arabian kingdoms in what is now Yemen. Because no trace of her has been found, her existence is disputed.

Sources differ on where she came from. Josephus made her queen of Egypt and Ethiopia, and the Talmud says that the phrase malkath Sheba means the kingdom of Sheba, not a woman. The New Testament mentions a queen of the South who came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon's wisdom, and in the Quran a speaker reports finding a woman ruling a people who bow to the sun instead of God.

Scholars date the biblical story variously. Many place its present form in the revision made during the Babylonian Captivity, about 550 BCE, and think its purpose was to glorify Solomon, although the Deuteronomic history is otherwise critical of him. The visit could conceivably have been a trade mission, since Solomon sought to settle on the Red Sea shore and so weaken the monopoly of Saba and other South Arabian kingdoms on the caravan trade, and Assyrian sources show that South Arabia traded internationally as early as 890 BCE.

The chronology is debated: Solomon lived from about 965 to 926 BCE, and some argue that the first traces of the Sabean monarchy come about 150 years later, though Peter Stein holds that the kingdom had emerged by the 10th century BCE.

South Arabian inscriptions mention a queen, but none names the Queen of Sheba, and excavations of the Sabaean temples of Awwām, known in folklore as the Sanctuary of Bilqis, found nothing connected with her. She became a popular subject of art. Twelfth-century cathedrals at Strasbourg, Chartres, Rochester and Canterbury show her, and in the Renaissance she appears on Ghiberti's doors of the Florence Baptistery and in Piero della Francesca's frescoes at Arezzo.
queen-victoria: Victoria was born on 24 May 1819, the daughter of Prince Edward, Duke of Kent and Strathearn, the fourth son of King George III. The death of Princess Charlotte of Wales in 1817 had caused a succession crisis that pressed the unmarried royal brothers to marry and have children. Victoria's father died in 1820, the year of her grandfather's death, and she was raised under close supervision by her mother and her mother's comptroller, John Conroy. She became heir presumptive when George IV died in 1830 and William IV succeeded him.

Victoria turned 18 on 24 May 1837, and William IV died on 20 June 1837, when she became queen. Her reign of 63 years and 216 days was longer than any of her predecessors' and gave its name to the Victorian era. On 10 February 1840 she married her maternal first cousin, Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha, having proposed to him herself on 15 October 1839. Their nine children married into royal and noble families across Europe, which earned her the name grandmother of Europe.

After Albert's death in 1861 she went into deep mourning and avoided public appearances. British republicanism briefly gained strength during her seclusion, but her popularity recovered in the latter half of her reign.

After the Indian Rebellion of 1857 the East India Company was dissolved, and Victoria condemned atrocities on both sides. The Royal Titles Act 1876 gave her the title Empress of India from 1 May 1876, proclaimed at the Delhi Durbar on 1 January 1877. Her Golden Jubilee in 1887 marked fifty years since her accession, and her Diamond Jubilee was also a time of public celebration.

Victoria died at Osborne House on the Isle of Wight on 22 January 1901, aged 81, and was succeeded by her son Edward VII; she was the last British monarch of the House of Hanover. From 1832 she kept a detailed journal that eventually ran to 122 volumes; after her death her youngest daughter Beatrice edited the diaries and burned the originals, though much of the text survives in copies. Of her grandchildren, 34 survived to adulthood. Her youngest son Leopold had haemophilia B, and her daughters Alice and Beatrice were carriers, so the disease passed to several royal houses of Europe. Her great-grandsons included Alexei Nikolaevich, Tsarevich of Russia, and Alfonso, Prince of Asturias.
quelimane: Quelimane is a seaport and the administrative capital of Zambezia Province in Mozambique, as well as the province's largest city. It stands 25 km from the mouth of the Rio dos Bons Sinais, the River of the Good Signs, which Vasco da Gama is said to have named when, on his way to India, he reached it and saw good signs that he was on the right path. The town and much of the province are extremely prone to floods in the rainy season.

The town began as a Swahili trade centre and then grew as a slave market of the Indian Ocean slave trade. It was founded by Muslim traders, with a link to the Kilwa Sultanate, and was one of the oldest towns in the region. The origin of its name is obscure. One tradition says that in 1498 Vasco da Gama asked some labourers for the name of the place and they answered kuliamani, meaning we are cultivating. Another says the Portuguese named the settlement after an Arab, or half-Arab, interpreter, since kalimani in the Arabic of the East African coast means interpreter.

In 1761 the settlement became a town. Until 1853 trade was forbidden to anyone but the Portuguese. In the early 20th century Swiss planters organised sisal plantations, and the town grew, attracting Muslim and Indian communities and new infrastructure built by the Portuguese authorities. Its port exported mainly tea from the district of Zambezia, and coconut was also processed there. By 1970 Quelimane had 71,786 inhabitants. The town was the end point of David Livingstone's west-to-east crossing of south-central Africa in 1856, and Mozambique became independent from Portugal in 1975.

Portuguese is the official language of Mozambique, and the most common local language around Quelimane is Chuabo. The town has a large hospital, two cathedrals, a mosque and a public university for teachers. It is the seat of a Roman Catholic diocese, and other Christian churches and mosques are also present.
quetzalcoatl: The name comes from Nahuatl and means Precious serpent or Quetzal-feathered Serpent. The earliest known depiction of a feathered serpent is on Stela 19 at the Olmec site of La Venta, dated to around 900 BCE, where a serpent rises behind a person who is probably engaged in a shamanic ritual. It is probably not the same deity as the later one, but it shows that feathered snakes were a symbol in Mesoamerica from the Formative period on.

Teotihuacan was the first culture to use the feathered serpent as an important religious and political symbol, notably at the Quetzalcoatl temple in the Ciudadela complex. The earliest images show a real snake; among the Classic Maya the figure began to take human features, such as a beard. After the fall of Teotihuacan, around 600 CE, the cult spread to Xochicalco, Cacaxtla and Cholula, and images then appear at Chichén Itzá and El Tajín. Cholula remained the chief centre of his worship in the Postclassic period.

Among the Aztecs Quetzalcoatl was a creator deity linked to wind, the planet Venus, the Sun, merchants, crafts and learning, and the patron of the priesthood. The two chief priests of the Templo Mayor bore the title Quetzalcoatl Tlamacazqui. As Ehecatl he is the wind; as the morning star he is called Tlahuizcalpantecuhtli, and his twin Xolotl is the evening star.

He descended to Mictlan, the underworld, and made the people of the fifth world from the bones of earlier races, using blood drawn from his own body. He is credited with inventing books and the calendar and with giving maize to humankind. In the Codex Chimalpopoca, Tezcatlipoca makes him drunk on pulque; ashamed, he burns himself in a stone chest, and his heart rises as the morning star.

Since the sixteenth century it has been widely held that Moctezuma II took Hernán Cortés, landing in 1519, for the returning Quetzalcoatl. Many scholars, among them Matthew Restall and James Lockhart, regard this as one of the myths of the Spanish conquest. They note that it appears only in documents of Spanish influence, such as the Florentine Codex, written some fifty years after the conquest. Franciscans such as Toribio de Benavente equated the god with Thomas the Apostle.

Between 1200 and 1600 a confederacy of Eastern Nahuas, Mixtecs and Zapotecs kept a pilgrimage and commercial centre at Cholula, which the Spaniards compared to Rome and Mecca. It fought the Aztec Empire for nearly seventy-five years and supplied the Spaniards with an army.
quetzaltenango: Quetzaltenango is the capital of the department of the same name in western Guatemala. It stands at an elevation of 2,330 metres in a high-altitude volcanic basin of the Sierra Madre, encircled by the volcanic complexes of Santa María, Santiaguito and Cerro Quemado. It is part of the Los Altos Metropolitan Area, which includes Salcajá, Cantel, Almolonga, Zunil and other municipalities.

The name is Nahuatl and means the walled place of the quetzal bird; it became the city's official name in colonial times. Many of its people, especially the indigenous population, use the Kʼicheʼ name Xelajú, or Xela, from xe laju' noj, meaning under ten mountains. Some consider it, unofficially, the capital of the Mayas.

Before the Spanish conquest Quetzaltenango was a city of the Mam Maya, though by 1524 it had become part of the Kʼicheʼ Kingdom of Qʼumarkaj. It was said to have been over 300 years old when the Spanish arrived. With the help of his allies, the conquistador Pedro de Alvarado defeated and killed the Maya ruler Tecún Umán there.

From 1838 to 1840 the city was the capital of the state of Los Altos, one of the states of the Federal Republic of Central America. As the union broke up, the army of Rafael Carrera conquered the city and made it part of Guatemala. In 1850 it had about 20,000 people, and wheat was its largest export, followed by cacao, sugar, wool and cotton. During the 19th century coffee was introduced as a major crop, the local economy prospered, and much Belle Époque architecture survives in the city.

On 24 October 1902 the Santa María volcano erupted, and rocks and ash fell on the city an hour later. In 1930 the only electric railway in Guatemala, the Ferrocarril de Los Altos, was inaugurated, built by AEG and Krupp and linking Quetzaltenango with San Felipe, Retalhuleu. Mudslides soon destroyed it and it was demolished in 1933. A railway museum now stands in the city centre.

Quetzaltenango is the main economic, educational and cultural centre of the south-western Guatemalan highlands. At the 2018 census it had 180,706 inhabitants, and 43 percent of its population was indigenous Guatemalan in 2014. It is home to several universities, among them the Centro Universitario de Occidente San Carlos de Guatemala, and to the football club Club Xelajú MC. In 2008 the Central American parliament, PARLACEN, announced that the city would be the capital of culture of Central America every 15 September.
qufu: Qufu is a county-level city in south-western Shandong, about 130 kilometres south of the provincial capital Jinan. Its name means crooked hill and refers to a mile-long hill that was part of the city when it was the capital of Lu. Together with Zoucheng, the birthplace of Mencius, it is known as Zoulu. Confucius is traditionally believed to have been born at nearby Mount Ni. The small historical centre is enclosed by a restored Ming-era city wall and moats.

In the Shang period the area was home to the people of Yan, counted among the Eastern Barbarians or Dongyi. After King Wu of Zhou founded the Zhou dynasty, his younger brother Dan, the Duke of Zhou, was granted the land and became Duke of Lu. He stayed at the royal court and entrusted the rule to his son Bo Qin. After the people of Yan joined a failed rebellion around 1042 BCE, their territory became part of Lu, which kept Qufu as its capital throughout the Spring and Autumn period. In 249 BCE Chu conquered Lu.

In 1012 the county was renamed Xianyuan and moved some 4 kilometres east. The Jin dynasty restored the name Qufu in 1142, but the city stayed on that site until 1522, when the Jiajing Emperor of the Ming had the present city wall built. In the Southern Song the head of the Confucius family, Duke Yansheng Kong Duanyou, fled south to Quzhou, while the Jin appointed his brother Kong Duancao as duke at Qufu. Two dukes existed until the Yuan period, when Kublai Khan invited the southern duke to return; he refused, and the northern branch kept the title. In November 1966, during the Cultural Revolution, about 200 staff members and students of Beijing Normal University destroyed more than 6,000 artefacts in the city.

The three best-known sites are the Temple of Confucius, the Cemetery of Confucius and the Kong Family Mansion, known together as San Kong and listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1994. The temple was consecrated by the Duke of Lu within two years of the death of Confucius. Its Dacheng Hall and nine courtyards on a central axis resemble the Forbidden City, and the complex has 460 rooms. The cemetery holds the tombs of more than 100,000 descendants of Confucius over about 2,000 years. In 1982 the State Council designated the city a national historical and cultural city.
quimper: Quimper is the prefecture of the Finistère department of Brittany in north-western France. It stands at the meeting of the Steir, Odet and Jet rivers, 62 km north-west of Lorient, 181 km west of Rennes and 486 km west-south-west of Paris. Its name comes from the Breton kemper, meaning confluence, a reference to the three rivers; the word is cognate with Welsh cymer. The Latin names were Civitas Aquilonia and Corisopitum, and the Breton name is Kemper. The climate is oceanic, with an average annual rainfall of about 1,214 mm.

The site was first settled in Roman times, when France was known as Gaul. By 495 it had become a bishopric, and the cathedral is dedicated to Corentin, a bishop of the fifth century and the first of Quimper. The town later became the capital of the counts of Cornouailles, the region of Cornouaille, which has a distinctive Breton-Celtic character; the historical name resembles that of Cornwall in southern England. In the eleventh century Cornouaille was united with the Duchy of Brittany.

The War of the Breton Succession (1341–1364) brought considerable ruin to the town, and in 1364 the duchy passed to the House of Montfort. Quimper's best-known product is Quimper faience, a tin-glazed pottery made here since 1690 using the bold provincial designs of Jean-Baptiste Bousquet. The town was also known for copper and bronze work, galvanised ironware, hosiery, leather, paper and woollen goods. In 1959 the commune absorbed the former communes of Ergué-Armel, Kerfunteun and Penhars. The physician René Laennec, inventor of the stethoscope, and the explorer Yves-Joseph de Kerguelen-Trémarec, who found the Kerguelen archipelago, were born in Quimper.

The Cathedral of Saint-Corentin was built between the thirteenth and sixteenth centuries and is the oldest Gothic structure in lower Brittany. Its twin towers are 76 m high, and the spires were added in the nineteenth century. The Romanesque Church of Locmaria dates from the eleventh century, and ruins of the fifteenth-century town walls stand near the Episcopal palace, which holds the Musée départemental Breton. The Musée des beaux-arts has paintings from the fourteenth to the twenty-first century, including works by Peter Paul Rubens and by painters of the Pont-Aven School.

Quimper keeps Breton traditions alive: its Diwan schools teach in Breton, and the Festival de Cornouaille is held in the last week of July. The railway station is the terminus of a high-speed TGV line from Paris, a journey of about 3 hours 40 minutes.
quintana-roo: Quintana Roo is Mexico's easternmost state, on the eastern part of the Yucatán Peninsula, with a coast on the Caribbean Sea to the east and the Gulf of Mexico to the north. It is bordered by Campeche to the west, Yucatán to the northwest and Belize to the south. Its capital is Chetumal, and it is divided into 11 municipalities. The state includes the city of Cancún, the islands of Cozumel and Isla Mujeres, the town of Bacalar and the Sian Ka'an biosphere reserve, and it has four generalised ecosystems: tropical forest, savanna, mangrove and coral reef. Its exposed position makes it frequently subject to severe hurricanes.

The area was long part of Yucatán and shared its history. From about 2000 BCE the Maya transformed it into an agricultural forest, managing selected trees, and archaeological evidence shows ancient home gardens, managed tree plots and cacao groves. Ancient human remains have been found in submerged caves and sinkholes near Tulum, including a woman who lived at least 9,900 years ago, found in the Chan Hol cave in 2016, one of the oldest human skeletons found on the American continent.

Spanish colonisation affected the region from the 16th century. With the Caste War of Yucatán, which began in the 1840s, all non-Indigenous peoples were driven from the region, and the independent Maya nation of Chan Santa Cruz, based on what is now the town of Felipe Carrillo Puerto, kept considerable independence for decades, with separate trade and treaty relationships with British Honduras, now Belize.

President Porfirio Díaz created the Territory of Quintana Roo by decree on 24 November 1902, naming it after Andrés Quintana Roo, an early patriot of the Mexican Republic. The Mexican Federal Army subdued most of the Maya population during the 1910s. In 1913 the area was declared part of Yucatán again, but in 1915 it became a separate territory once more, and on 8 October 1974 it was granted statehood.

In the last quarter of the 20th century tourism, above all the development of Cancún, drove rapid growth in the north of the state, while the south kept a traditional economy of forestry and wood extraction. Many migrants have come from Yucatán, Campeche, Tabasco and Veracruz. The state holds the Maya sites of Chacchoben, Cobá, Kohunlich, Muyil, Tulum, Xel-Há, San Gervasio and Xcaret.
quintus-caecilius-metellus-macedonicus: Metellus was the oldest son of Quintus Caecilius Metellus and the grandson of Lucius Caecilius Metellus. After his praetorship in 148 BCE and his consulship in 143 BCE he was proconsul of Hispania Citerior in 142 BCE and censor in 131 BCE. He took his agnomen, Macedonicus, from his victory over the Macedonians. Under his authority Macedonia was reduced and made a Roman province.

In 148 BCE, as praetor, Metellus defeated Andriscus twice. Andriscus claimed to be a son of Perseus, the last king of the Antigonid dynasty, and had risen against Rome with an army recruited from Thrace. In 146 BCE Metellus defeated Critolaos of Megalopolis at the Battle of Scarpheia and the Arcadians at Chaeronea, and then fought in the Achaean War under the consul Lucius Mummius Achaicus. Mummius's victory over the Achaean League delayed the triumph that Scarpheia merited, but Metellus received it on his return to Italy.

He later built the Portico of Metellus beside the Circus Flaminius, with temples of Jupiter Stator and Juno, the first marble temples in Rome, and adorned them with Lysippus's equestrian statues of the generals of Alexander the Great. Whether he also built the temple of Juno is disputed. As consul in 143 and 142 BCE he campaigned against the Celtiberians in the Numantine War, defeating the Arevaci, Lusones, Belli, Titii and Vaccaei, but did not confront Numantia, which then held out for ten years.

In 133 BCE he spoke against Tiberius Gracchus, who planned to put the fortune of the late Attalus III of Pergamon, bequeathed to the Roman people, under the control of the Plebeian Assembly and so bypass the senate. As censor he pledged to halt the decay of Roman custom and proposed that marriage be compulsory for all citizens.

His moralizing aroused popular opposition led by the tribune Gaius Atinius Labeo Macerio, whom he had expelled from the senate, and he was almost killed by the mob on the Tarpeian Rock. A century later Augustus had his speech on marriage read in the senate and published as an edict. Metellus quarrelled with Scipio Aemilianus but mourned his death and ordered his sons to carry the body to the pyre.

Contemporary and later sources describe him as a prominent Roman who held many civil and military offices. Four of his sons reached the consulship, as did his sons-in-law Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica and Gaius Servilius Vatia. A painting by Armand-Charles Caraffe commemorates the legend that he lifted the siege of Centobrigia in 142 BCE to spare the lives of innocents.
quintus-caecilius-metellus-numidicus: Metellus Numidicus, born about 155 BCE, was the son of Lucius Caecilius Metellus Calvus. In his youth he was sent to Athens, where he studied under the philosopher Carneades, a master of oratory, and he returned cultured and a brilliant speaker. His career ran from quaestor in 126 BCE to tribune of the plebs in 121 BCE, aedile in 118 BCE, praetor in 115 BCE and governor of Sicily in 114 BCE. Accused of extortion when he left the province, he was acquitted at once, the judges being so sure of his good character that they dismissed the case without examining it. He supported the arts and sponsored his friend the poet Archias.

Elected consul for 109 BCE with Marcus Junius Silanus, Metellus took command of the war in Numidia against Jugurtha. The campaign dragged on, and he won one important victory, at the Battle of the Muthul. His command was prolonged, and he stayed in Numidia through 108 BCE besieging Jugurthine strongholds. His second-in-command, Gaius Marius, spread rumours that Metellus was prolonging the war to keep his command, returned to Rome, won the consulship for 107 BCE and took over the war. Metellus was met in Rome with enthusiasm from senators and people who did not support Marius, and he was granted a triumph and the name Numidicus, to Marius's irritation.

He became the chief leader of the aristocratic faction against the rise of Marius, whom the people favoured for finishing the war with the capture of Jugurtha, thanks to a stratagem of Sulla. As censor in 102 BCE he tried and failed to expel Marius's ally Lucius Appuleius Saturninus from the Senate. Saturninus, as tribune, then proposed with Marius an agrarian law giving land to veterans, with a clause requiring every senator to swear to uphold it on pain of expulsion and a heavy fine. Marius and every other senator swore, but Metellus refused, resigned his seat and paid the fine.

Saturninus then proposed a law exiling Metellus. Rather than let his supporters, who were ready to defend him by force, clash with those of Saturninus, he left voluntarily and spent a year at Rhodes, studying philosophy in the company of the rhetorician Lucius Aelius Praeconinus, called Stilo. After Saturninus died, the tribune Quintus Calidius proposed his recall in 99 BCE, and his son earned the name Pius by his efforts for the proposal. Metellus lived out his years in Rome, rarely taking part in public affairs. Cicero records, without confidence, a rumour that the tribune Quintus Varius poisoned him. He had a reputation for integrity at a time when Roman politics was growing more corrupt.
quintus-caecilius-metellus-pius: Metellus Pius belonged to the plebeian gens Caecilia and was the son of Quintus Caecilius Metellus Numidicus, consul in 109 BCE. He accompanied his father to Numidia during the Jugurthine War. When Numidicus was banished through the manoeuvres of Gaius Marius and Lucius Appuleius Saturninus, the son campaigned for his recall, petitioning in 99 BCE, and in 98 BCE the tribune Quintus Calidius carried a law that allowed Numidicus to return. His persistence earned him the nickname Pius. In the 90s BCE he was elected to the College of Pontiffs, and in the Social War he served as a legate, winning battles against the Marsi.

Elected praetor in 88 BCE, Metellus Pius enrolled the Italian allies as Roman citizens and then took the southern front, capturing Venusia and defeating the rebel leader Quintus Poppaedius Silo. When Cinna and Marius took Rome in 87 BCE he left for Africa and acted as governor there until the Marians sent out Gaius Fabius Hadrianus in 84 BCE, who drove him out. By 83 BCE he had joined Lucius Cornelius Sulla, who made him his principal subordinate, and the Senate declared him a public enemy. In 82 BCE he defeated Marian forces in northern Italy, with the young Pompey as his cavalry commander. Sulla made him pontifex maximus in 81 BCE and consul beside himself in 80 BCE.

In 79 BCE the Senate sent him to Hispania Ulterior to fight the rebel Quintus Sertorius. Sertorius's guerrilla tactics defeated Metellus repeatedly, and by 77 BCE the Senate sent Pompey with a large army to help. Metellus defeated Sertorius's legate Lucius Hirtuleius at the Battle of Italica in 75 BCE, and was acclaimed imperator after a battle near Segontia in which he was wounded by a spear. He offered 100 silver talents and 20,000 acres to any Roman who would betray Sertorius, who was murdered in 72 BCE. His governorship ended in 71 BCE, and he held a triumph with Pompey on 30 December 71 BCE.

In the 60s BCE Metellus Pius opposed Pompey's extraordinary commands, and he was one of the former consuls called as witnesses against Pompey's associate Gaius Cornelius when he was charged with maiestas. He was a friend and patron of the poet Aulus Licinius Archias. He died around 63 BCE, and Julius Caesar succeeded him that year as pontifex maximus. He had no natural children, and by his will he adopted a son of Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica, who became Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius Scipio Nasica, consul in 52 BCE and father-in-law of Pompey.
quintus-curtius-rufus: Apart from his name on the manuscripts, nothing about Curtius Rufus is definitely known. His Histories is isolated in Roman literature, since no other ancient text is known to mention either the work or its author. Its date rests wholly on internal evidence. Book X praises the blessings of peace under Roman imperial rule, and its mention of the Parthian Empire, which lasted from 247 BCE to 224 CE, gives outer limits. A passage contrasting the succession crises of Alexander's generals with a Roman civil war averted by the quick appointment of an emperor has been read as the night of 24-25 January 41 CE, when Claudius was declared emperor. Many modern scholars accept the middle to late first century CE.

By his name he would have belonged to the Curtii Rufi, a branch of an old patrician family. One plausible candidate is a Curtius Rufus who was consul suffectus from October to December 43 CE under Claudius. Tacitus has him serving on the staff of a quaestor in Africa and as a protégé of Tiberius, and implies that he may have been of low birth.

His Historiae Alexandri Magni, the Histories of Alexander the Great, was written in ten books. Books I and II are entirely missing, with further gaps in Books V, VI and X. The work survives in 123 codices, all derived from one incomplete exemplar of the ninth century. It rarely names its sources, though it mentions Cleitarchus twice and Ptolemy and Timagenes once each; works built on such accounts are grouped as the Vulgate tradition of Alexander historiography. Peter Pratt has suggested that it was left unpublished because of its themes of conquest, rebellion and imperial ambition.

The work became popular in the High Middle Ages and was a principal source for the Alexander Romance, including Walter of Châtillon's epic poem Alexandreis. It was admired in the Italian Renaissance, and painters such as Paolo Veronese and Charles Le Brun drew on episodes from it. The first printed edition was made at Venice by Vindelinus Spirensis in 1470 or 1471, and Edmund Hedicke's edition of 1867 set a convention that remains influential.
quintus-petillius-cerialis: His full name was Quintus Petillius Cerialis Caesius Rufus. Because he probably followed Caesius Nasica in command of the Ninth Legion, and brothers often held the same post in turn, Anthony Birley has suggested that he was Nasica's younger brother, adopted by Petillius Rufus, praetor in 28 CE. Olli Salomies argues instead that he was the natural son of Petillius Rufus by a woman named Caesia, which would make Nasica a close relative rather than a brother. He married Domitilla the Younger, daughter of Vespasian.

His first major post was as legate of Legio IX Hispana in Britain under the governor Gaius Suetonius Paulinus. During the rising of Boudica of the Iceni in 60 or 61 he marched to relieve Camulodunum, modern Colchester, which the Britons had already taken. In the words of Tacitus, the enemy routed his troops and destroyed all his infantry, and he escaped with some cavalry to his camp, where its fortifications saved him.

In the civil wars of 69, the Year of the Four Emperors, Vitellius held him as a hostage, but he escaped disguised as a peasant and joined the Flavian army, leading cavalry into Rome along the Via Salaria. He was then given command against the Batavian rising in Germania Inferior, where tribes under Julius Civilis, a romanised prince, had besieged two legions at Xanten. His victory brought honours from Vespasian, among them his first consulship.

Governing Britain from 71, he brought Legio II Adiutrix with him and was supported by Gnaeus Julius Agricola, commander of Legio XX Valeria Victrix. A military diploma of 21 May 74 shows him consul a second time, with Titus Clodius Eprius Marcellus as colleague. He was still alive after 83. Tacitus judged him a bold soldier rather than a careful general, ready to stake everything on one battle, with a natural eloquence that appealed to his troops and an unshakable loyalty to his superiors.
quintus-sertorius: Quintus Sertorius was born in Nursia, in Sabine territory, around 126 BCE into a family of equestrian status. As the first of his family to enter the Senate he was a novus homo. His father died before he came of age, and his mother Rhea saw that he received the best education possible. In his mid-to-late teens he moved to Rome to make a career as an orator and jurist; his blunt, bold style made enough impression on the young Cicero for a mention in a later treatise.

He served under Gaius Marius against the Germanic tribes, probably spying on them in disguise, and was elected quaestor in 92 BCE, governing Cisalpine Gaul in 91 BCE as the Social War began. After Sulla blocked his attempt at the tribunate about 88 BCE, Sertorius joined Cinna and Marius in the civil war, and was probably praetor in 85 or 84 BCE.

Sent to Hispania as proconsul by late 83 or early 82 BCE, Sertorius could not persuade the Spanish tribes to fight for him. Proscribed by Sulla and outnumbered, he abandoned his provinces, sailed with 3,000 followers to Mauretania and then joined Cilician pirates, who took Pityussa in the Balearic Islands, before he fled the islands. In 80 BCE he crossed from Tingis to Baelo, was reinforced by Lusitanians and defeated Lucius Fufidius at the Battle of the Baetis River.

The Senate sent Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius, whom Sertorius called the old woman. Using guerrilla warfare, Sertorius outmanoeuvred him, and his humane administration, which treated the natives as allies, drew many to his cause; they called him the new Hannibal, since he also had one eye. He also used a tamed white fawn to claim divine favour. Pompey was given an extraordinary command against him, but late in 77 BCE Marcus Perperna Veiento joined Sertorius with fifty-three cohorts, which allowed open battles. Pompey defeated Perperna at Valentia in 75 BCE, and Sertorius fought him at Sucro before returning to guerrilla war.

Metellus offered a hundred talents of silver and twenty thousand iugera of land to any Roman who killed Sertorius. He grew paranoid and replaced his Roman bodyguard with an Iberian one, which was unpopular among his Roman followers. Perperna organised a banquet at Osca in 73 or 72 BCE, kept the Spanish guards outside, and with other conspirators murdered him.

Iberian support collapsed, and Pompey and Metellus soon crushed Perperna's army. Ancient sources concede that Sertorius was a great military leader, and Appian, who was hostile, thought the war would not have ended so soon had he lived. His motives cannot really be known, but evidence suggests he fought for those disinherited and proscribed after Sulla's victory in 82 BCE.
quintus-tullius-cicero: Quintus Tullius Cicero was born into a well-to-do equestrian family of Arpinum, about 100 kilometres south-east of Rome. His father arranged for him to be educated with his brother Marcus in Rome, Athens and probably Rhodes in 79 to 77 BCE. Around 70 BCE he married Pomponia, the sister of Marcus's friend Titus Pomponius Atticus, a woman of strong personality. The marriage was long and disharmonious, and he divorced her in late 45 BCE despite several attempts by Marcus to reconcile them. They had a son, also named Quintus, born in 66 BCE.

Quintus was aedile in 66 BCE, praetor in 62 BCE and propraetor of the province of Asia for three years from 61 to 59 BCE. In Asia he was honest in a post where many Romans amassed private property, but he inflicted old-fashioned punishments, such as drowning a convicted parricide in a sack. During the Gallic Wars he served as a legate under Caesar, accompanied him on his second expedition to Britain in 54 BCE and survived a Nervian siege of his camp during the revolt of Ambiorix.

Caesar described him as a brave soldier who rallied his legion at a critical moment. In 51 BCE he served as legate under his brother, governor of Cilicia. In Caesar's civil war he supported the Pompeian faction, and later obtained Caesar's pardon.

He had an impulsive temperament and fits of cruelty in operations, which Romans of the time frowned on. Marcus wrote to Atticus in 51 BCE that he dared not leave him alone. Quintus enjoyed Greek tragedy and wrote four tragedies in the Greek style, among them Troades, Erigona and Electra, all lost. Three letters to Tiro survive, and the Commentariolum Petitionis, a handbook on electioneering, which Andrew Lintott has argued is his, though its authenticity has been questioned.

The brothers were close, apart from a serious disagreement during Caesar's dictatorship from 49 to 44 BCE, and Marcus's letters to Quintus show their affection. When the Second Triumvirate proscribed Quintus, his son and his brother in 43 BCE, Quintus fled from Tusculum with Marcus, then went home for travelling money. His son hid him and refused to reveal the hiding place even under torture. Hearing of this, Quintus gave himself up to try to save his son, but father, son and Marcus were all killed in 43 BCE.
quipu: The word quipu comes from a Quechua word meaning 'knot'; khipu is the spelling that reflects Quechua and Aymara. A claim that a proto-quipu exists at the Late Preceramic site of Caral, from about 3000-1800 BCE, has not been thoroughly evaluated. A more plausible precursor is the wrapped batons from Cerrillos of the Late Paracas period, about 350-200 BCE. The first undisputed quipus belong to the Middle Horizon, about 600-1000 CE, and are attributed to the Wari Empire. Wari specimens tend to be smaller and have brightly coloured thread wrapped around the cords, and they used a system of knots that scholars do not fully understand.

A quipu usually consists of cotton or camelid fibre cords and holds information sorted by dimensions such as colour, order and number. It can have anything from a few cords to several thousand. In the numerical system Leslie Leland Locke first showed, and Marcia Ascher and Robert Ascher later analysed on several hundred examples, knots are tied in clusters along the cord and the position of a cluster gives a power of ten.

Simple knots in a row stand for tens and higher digits, a long knot with extra turns for the digits 2 to 9 in the ones position, a figure-eight knot for 1, and the absence of a knot for zero. So 731 is written as 7s, 3s and E.

How non-numerical information was recorded is disputed. Gary Urton has suggested a binary system that could record phonological or logographic data, while Frank Salomon argues for a system of representative symbols. A 2005 report identified a sequence of three figure-eight knots at the start of a quipu that may name Puruchuco, its keeper or its subject.

Under the Inca Empire, specialists called quipucamayocs made and read quipus. They carried out addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, tracked the mita labour tax and economic output, ran the census and kept the calendar. Inca historians also used quipus when they told the Spanish about the past, though it is unknown whether the cords held the story itself or only key numbers.

After the Spanish conquest began in 1532, officials at first relied on quipus to settle disputes over tribute, and quipucamayocs could be summoned to court. The Third Council of Lima ordered some burned in 1583 as idolatrous because they recorded offerings to non-Christian gods. Some priests promoted their use, and quipu boards joined knots with writing. Just under 1,400 pre-Columbian quipus are known today, and some Andean villages still display them as communal heritage.
quirigua: Quiriguá is a medium-sized site of about 3 square kilometres, with its ceremonial centre about a kilometre from the north bank of the lower Motagua River. It lies 48 kilometres north of Copán. The river has since changed course and now flows a kilometre south of the centre, and the flood plain exposed the site to periodic flooding.

The local bedrock is a hard red sandstone that does not shear or fracture easily, which let sculptors erect the tallest freestanding stone monuments in the Americas. It stood where the trade route from the highlands to the Caribbean coast met the route from Copán to the Petén cities, and it could control the trade in uncut jade, cacao and obsidian along the river.

Late Preclassic artifacts show occupation before 200 CE, and the acropolis was begun by about 550. No monuments were raised from 495 to 653. In the 6th or early 7th century a flood buried the surface of the site in silt, and a smaller complex became the new centre. The first new monument in a century and a half was raised in 653 by the king K'awiil Yopaat.

In 724 Uaxaclajuun Ub'aah K'awiil of Copán installed K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat on the throne of Quiriguá as his vassal. By 734 the king called himself k'ul ahaw, 'holy lord', and in 736 he received a visit from Wamaw K'awiil, the high king of Calakmul, which suggests that Calakmul backed his rebellion in order to weaken Tikal, an old ally of Copán. In 738 he captured the Copán king, who was sacrificed in the Great Plaza at Quiriguá. The city kept its independence, and its population and building grew rapidly, though the population never exceeded about 1,200 to 1,600 in the centre.

The city's power waned under its last recorded ruler, Jade Sky, whose two stelae are stunted. The last hieroglyphic texts date from 810, when Yax Pasaj Chan Yopaat of Copán visited to carry out a k'atun-ending ritual. Quiriguá then lost its reason to exist as trade stopped flowing along the Motagua, and it was nearly deserted within a few years. People linked to the Yucatán coast briefly reoccupied it in the early Postclassic, about 900 to 1200, and added to the acropolis.

Quiriguá lies in the municipality of Los Amates, department of Izabal, in south-eastern Guatemala, a little over 200 kilometres north-east of Guatemala City. It has been on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1981.
quit-india-movement: In 1939 the Governor-General, Lord Linlithgow, brought India into World War II without consulting Indian nationalists. The Muslim League supported the war, while Congress was divided. In September 1939 the Congress Working Committee offered conditional support for the fight against the Axis but was rebuffed when it asked for independence in return, and Congress ministers in eight provinces resigned. Gandhi's individual civil disobedience campaign of 1940–41 led to the arrest of almost fourteen thousand satyagrahis.

In March 1942 the British sent Stafford Cripps to India to win Congress cooperation in return for devolution to an elected legislature. The talks failed because the offer, essentially limited dominion status after the war, did not give a timetable for self-government. Gandhi called it a post-dated cheque on a crashing bank. The threat of Japanese invasion also pushed national leaders to doubt that the British could defend India.

The Congress Working Committee at Wardha adopted a resolution on 14 July 1942 demanding complete independence and threatening mass civil disobedience. It was controversial: Chakravarti Rajagopalachari left Congress over it, and Nehru and Maulana Azad had doubts but stayed with Gandhi. The All India Congress Committee met in Bombay and on 8 August 1942 Gandhi gave his Do or Die speech at the Gowalia Tank Maidan. Almost the entire Congress leadership was imprisoned without trial within hours. The Muslim League, the Hindu Mahasabha, the Communist Party of India, the Indian Civil Service and some princely states did not support the campaign.

Leaderless protests spread, with strikes, boycotts and sabotage. From 9 August to 21 September 1942, according to John F. Riddick, protesters attacked 550 post offices and 250 railway stations, destroyed 70 police stations, and cut telegraph wires about 2,500 times. Violence was most intense in Bihar. In Tamluk and Contai in Midnapore a parallel government, the Tamluk National Government, lasted until 1944, and at Ballia people overthrew the district administration for some weeks. The British deployed 57 battalions of troops. Linlithgow called it by far the most serious rebellion since 1857.

The British made over 100,000 arrests, imposed mass fines and used public flogging, and hundreds of civilians were killed, many shot by police or soldiers. Leaders such as Aruna Asaf Ali and Achyut Rao Patwardhan went underground, broadcasting over clandestine radio. The Congress leadership was cut off from the world for over three years. Gandhi was released in 1944 because of his health. The movement ended in 1945 with the release of all jailed nationalists, after the Labour Party won the British election that year promising independence for India.
quito: Quito lies in the northern highlands of Ecuador, in the Guayllabamba river basin, on a long plateau on the eastern flanks of Pichincha, an active stratovolcano. The valley is flanked by volcanoes, some of them snow-capped. Pichincha has several summits, among them Ruku Pichincha at 4,700 metres and Guagua Pichincha at 4,794 metres. The city is about 40 kilometres long and five kilometres wide at its widest, so its main avenues run from north to south. Because of its altitude and its position on the equator the climate is cool and fairly constant, with a dry season from June to August and a wet season from September to May.

The oldest traces of human presence near Quito were excavated in 1960 by the American archaeologist Robert E. Bell at El Inga, on the slopes of the Ilaló volcano. Hunter-gatherers left obsidian tools there that are dated to 8000 BCE. Settled populations are thought to have lived in the area between 4400 and 1600 BCE. In the late fifteenth century the Inca Emperor Huayna Capac defeated the Quitu, the region's original inhabitants, and made Quito the capital of the empire's northern region.

Inca resistance to the Spanish continued in 1534. Diego de Almagro founded Santiago de Quito on 15 August 1534 at Colta, near Riobamba, and renamed it San Francisco de Quito on 28 August. The city was refounded at its present site on 6 December 1534 by 204 settlers led by Sebastián de Benalcázar, who captured the leader Rumiñahui, effectively ending organized resistance. Rumiñahui was executed on 10 January 1535. The Spanish conquest of 1534 is the date most often cited as the city's official founding, which makes Quito the oldest capital in South America.

In the republican period Quito saw political violence. Members of the Society of Free Inhabitants of Quito were assassinated by the government in 1833 after conspiring against it, and the Marcist Revolution began on 6 March 1845. President Gabriel García Moreno was assassinated in the city in 1875, and Archbishop José Ignacio Checa y Barba was killed by poison while celebrating Mass in 1877.

Quito is the capital of Ecuador and of Pichincha province, and the country's major governmental, administrative and cultural institutions are within it. Its historic centre, on 320 hectares, is the largest, least altered and best preserved in the Americas, with about 130 monumental buildings of mostly religious art and sculpture. It was declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO on 18 September 1978, together with Kraków as the first to be so named. The equator runs through the northern part of the metropolitan area.
quotations-from-chairman-mao-tse-tung: The book grew out of Lin Biao's practice of building the study of Mao Zedong's texts into the daily drills of the People's Liberation Army. In 1961 Lin required the PLA Daily to print a Mao quotation each day, using an index of Mao's quotes arranged by topic that the Tianjin Daily had made, and this index became the core of the book. In December 1963 a deputy editor-in-chief of the PLA Daily proposed a selection in book form, and the first draft was 200 Quotations from Chairman Mao.

In May 1964 the General Political Department issued an internal edition with 355 quotations under 30 topics, and endorsement leaves written by Lin Biao. The definitive 1965 version has 427 quotations in 33 thematic chapters, taken from Mao's speeches and writings of 1929 to 1964 and drawing heavily on about two dozen documents in the four volumes of his Selected Works. From August 1965 copies had red vinyl covers, and most editions were small enough for a pocket.

The first print run of 4.2 million copies went only to the army, and 12 million had been printed by August 1965. In August 1966 the People's Publishing House took over printing and sold the book through Xinhua Bookstores, and provinces were ordered to build hundreds of new printing houses. On National Day in 1966 one million copies were handed to Red Guards who had travelled to Beijing, and people often swore oaths on the book.

It was approved for export in 1966 and, by May 1967, bookstores in 117 countries and territories were distributing it, in more than 50 languages. From the mid-1960s to the mid-1970s it was the most printed book in the world, and sources put the total at billions of copies.

Emphasis on the book decreased after the 9th Party Congress in April 1969. On 12 February 1979 the Publicity Department of the Chinese Communist Party ordered publication stopped, stating that the book distorted Mao Zedong Thought and had a widespread and pernicious influence. Today it is mostly nostalgia in China and is hard to find in bookstores. Abroad it was taken up in the French Maoist context, by African American and Asian American radicals in the United States, who sold copies in Berkeley in 1967, and in India by Charu Majumdar in the Naxalite movement.
quran: Muslims believe the Quran was revealed orally by God to Muhammad through the angel Gabriel over some 23 years, ending in 632 CE, the year of his death. Islamic tradition relates that the first revelation came in 610 CE in the Cave of Hira, on the Laylat al-Qadr, during one of his retreats to the mountains. According to tradition, several of Muhammad's companions served as scribes. Shortly after his death the Quran was compiled on the order of the first caliph, Abu Bakr, by companions who had written down or memorised parts of it. The caliph Uthman, who reigned from 644 to 656, established a standard version, the Uthmanic codex, which is generally considered the archetype of the Quran known today.

Some scholars argue that manuscript evidence, textual variants such as the Sanaa manuscript, and historical sources suggest a more gradual and complex process of compilation. Some textual critics hold that there never was a single original text, and Sunni and Shia accounts of its origins differ. Canonical variant readings, the qirāʾāt, are transmitted orally and differ only slightly in wording.

The text has 114 chapters, called sūrahs, made up of verses, called āyahs. The most popular Hafs version has 6,236 verses. The chapters are not in chronological order but roughly in order of decreasing size, and each except the ninth begins with the Bismillah, 'In the name of God'. Traditional accounts classify chapters as Meccan or Medinan, depending on whether they were revealed before or after Muhammad's migration to Medina.

The content covers basic beliefs such as the existence of God and the resurrection, narratives of earlier prophets, ethical and legal subjects, events of Muhammad's time, charity and prayer. Its style is allusive: events are referred to but not narrated, and people and places are mentioned but rarely named. For this reason Muslims rely on tafsir, or commentary, to explain it, together with the hadiths, oral traditions believed to record the words and actions of Muhammad.

In prayer the Quran is recited only in Arabic, ideally with a special prosody called tajwid. A person who has memorised the whole text is called a hafiz. Before printing was widely adopted in the 19th century it was copied by hand. The earliest manuscripts were in Hijazi script, and Kufic scripts with thicker strokes probably appeared in the ninth century. From the 11th century naskh, muhaqqaq and rayḥānī styles dominated, with the Maghribī style popular in North Africa and Iberia. Because copies were costly, they were often kept in mosques, frequently as a series of 30 parts, and Ottoman copyists were highly productive. Translating the text has always been considered difficult, since an Arabic word may have a range of meanings depending on context.
quraysh: According to traditional Arab sources, the Quraysh descend from Fihr ibn Malik, of the Kinana tribe, whose line is traced back to Adnan the Ishmaelite, regarded in tradition as the father of the northern Arabs. The tribe gained its name when Qusayy ibn Kilab, a sixth-generation descendant of Fihr, gathered his kinsmen and took control of the Kaaba, then a major pagan sanctuary in Mecca. Medieval Muslim sources agree that he made the Quraysh the dominant power in Mecca and assigned quarters to the clans. At first the Meccan economy rested on pilgrimage to the Kaaba rather than trade, and a dispute over his succession split the tribe into two factions.

Toward the end of the 6th century the Quraysh and Kinana fought the Fijar War against Qaysi tribes, whose aim, according to W. Montgomery Watt, was control of the trade routes of Najd. By about 600 CE the Quraysh leaders were prosperous merchants with something like a monopoly of the trade between the Indian Ocean and East Africa on one side and the Mediterranean on the other. They sent caravans to Yemen in winter and to Gaza, Bosra and Damascus in summer. The clans of Makhzum and Umayya acquired the most wealth, and the Umayyads were the strongest.

Muhammad was born into the Banu Hashim. The Quraysh at first showed little concern at his preaching but opposed him as he challenged the polytheism of Mecca. After the Hijra to Medina they fought him at Badr, Uhud and the Trench. A ten-year truce, the Treaty of al-Hudaybiya, was broken when a group among the Quraysh, against the advice of their chief Abu Sufyan, supported a client clan against allies of Muhammad. Muhammad entered Mecca virtually unopposed in 630, and almost all its inhabitants adopted Islam.

Muhammad brought the Quraysh into the ruling elite of the Muslim community, and the historian Fred Donner suggests that their organisational skills improved his statecraft in his last years.
