After his death in 632 a hadith holding that the caliph must come from the Quraysh became almost universally accepted, except among the Kharijites, and control of the state became a struggle between Qurayshi factions: the Banu Umayya under Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, the Banu Hashim under Ali, and others. The Umayyads won the Second Fitna in 692 or 693. In 750 the Abbasids, a branch of the Banu Hashim, defeated them and killed many of the Banu Umayya.
qusayr-amra: Qusayr 'Amra, also written Quseir Amra or Qasr Amra, is the best known of the desert castles of eastern Jordan. It stands on the north side of Highway 40, about 85 kilometres from Amman and 21 kilometres south-west of Al-Azraq. What survives is the remnant of a larger complex of about 25 hectares that included a castle meant as a royal retreat, without military function, of which only the foundation remains. Its placement was governed by access to the ancient routes running north from Arabia to Syria, including the one from Tayma through Wadi Sirhan to the plain of Balqa.

A painting of six kings that includes the Visigothic king Roderic, who reigned 710 to 712, led researchers for a long time to date the building to about 710 and to the caliph Walid I. An inscription found in 2012 dated it to the two decades from 723 to 743, when it was commissioned by Walid ibn Yazid, crown prince under the caliph Hisham and caliph himself in 743 and 744. Walid and Yazid, two princes who each later became caliph, spent long periods away from Damascus, the Umayyad capital, before taking the throne.

The surviving building is a small hall and bathhouse of limestone and basalt, made of rough masonry bound with gypsum-lime mortar in a Sasanian tradition. The bathhouse is one of the oldest surviving remains of a hammam in the historic Muslim world. Its frescoes, mostly on the ceilings, show hunting, bathing and dancing scenes, working craftsmen, animals and plants, and a cycle of Jonah, the earliest known images of Jonah in Islamic art. The six kings are identified as the Byzantine emperor, Roderic, the Sasanian shah, the Negus of Ethiopia and the emperor of China, and their meaning is unclear, though a Greek word for victory found nearby suggests the caliph's supremacy over his enemies.

The hemispherical dome of the hot room shows the zodiac and 35 identifiable constellations, believed to be the earliest image of the night sky painted on anything other than a flat surface. Its only discernible error, the counterclockwise order of the stars, suggests it was copied from a flat original.

Alois Musil rediscovered the abandoned building in 1898, and drawings of the frescoes by Alphons Leopold Mielich in his book made them known. A Spanish team restored the frescoes in the 1970s, and the shellac applied then was removed in 1996. UNESCO inscribed the site as a World Heritage Site in 1985. A conservation project begun in 2010 by the World Monuments Fund, an Italian institute and the Department of Antiquities of Jordan also covers the exterior buildings, and cleaning has revealed rich colours.
qusayy-ibn-kilab: Qusayy, born Zayd and the son of Kilab ibn Murrah, lived according to tradition from about 400 to 480. Islamic tradition makes him a descendant of Abraham through Ishmael. His father died when he was an infant, and his mother, Fatimah bint Sa'd ibn Sayl, married Rabi'ah ibn Haram of the Bani Azra, who took her to Syria, where she bore a son called Darraj. Qusayy grew up treating Rabi'ah as his father until a quarrel with members of Rabi'ah's tribe showed that they did not count him as one of their own. His mother then told him that he was the son of Kilab ibn Murrah, whose people lived near the Holy House in Mecca, and he returned there.

In Mecca the trustee and guardian of the Kaaba was Hulail ibn Hubshiyyah, chief of the Banu Khuza'a, whose daughter Hubbah Qusayy married. Tradition holds that Hulail preferred Qusayy to his own sons as successor, and by his will Qusayy received the trusteeship of the Kaaba after him. Qusayy then settled his nearest kin of Quraysh in the valley beside the sanctuary, among them his brother Zuhrah and his uncle Taym ibn Murrah; they and their descendants were called the Quraysh of the Hollow, while more distant kinsmen in the surrounding hills were the Quraysh of the Outskirts.

He ruled as a king. He rebuilt the Kaaba from a state of decay, had the Arab people build their houses around it, and built a House of Assembly where clan leaders met to discuss social, commercial and political matters. He laid down that pilgrims be supplied with food and water, paid for by a tax, and divided the duties of caring for pilgrims and the Kaaba, of war and of keeping peace among the tribes.

Among his sons were Abd, Abd-al-Dar, Abd Manaf and Abd-al-Uzza. Abd Manaf was honoured in his father's lifetime, but Qusayy preferred his first-born, Abd-al-Dar, and shortly before his death handed him all his rights and powers and the House of Assembly. Besides Muhammad, the caliphs Uthman and Ali and the later Umayyad, Abbasid and Fatimid caliphs descended from him, and many dynasties from Morocco to Brunei have claimed descent from him.
qutayba-ibn-muslim: Qutayba was born at Basra into the Bahila tribe. His father, Muslim ibn Amr, fought for an enemy of the Umayyad Caliphate Mus'ab ibn al-Zubayr and was killed at the Battle of Maskin, but first obtained a promise of safety for his son from Caliph Abd al-Malik.

Qutayba came to the notice of al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf during the suppression of the revolt of Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad ibn al-Ash'ath and took Rayy in 701. Al-Hajjaj chose him as governor of Khurasan partly because the Bahila belonged to neither of the feuding Yemeni and Qaysi tribal confederations, and partly because he had no strong tribal base and would stay loyal to his patron.

Qutayba spent about ten years in Central Asia. Earlier Arab expeditions across the Oxus had been raids for booty, and the local princes were divided among themselves. He retook Balkh in 705 and then spent 706 to 709 on Bukhara. After he sacked Baykand, executing the men of fighting age and selling the women and children, the Sogdian princes united against him, and only a direct assault in 709 took Bukhara.

He also raised native Khurasani auxiliary levies to supplement his Arab army. In Khwarizm his forces massacred the upper classes who had fomented revolt, and al-Biruni compared the destruction of its manuscripts to a barbarian sack. At Samarkand he granted lenient terms and then garrisoned the city, which damaged his standing among the Sogdians. From 713 he campaigned along the Jaxartes valley, and sources report a raid on Kashgar that some modern historians doubt.

After al-Hajjaj died in 714 Qutayba's position weakened. When Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik succeeded al-Walid I, Qutayba, who had argued against Sulayman's succession, feared dismissal and resolved to rebel. The Khurasani Arabs refused to follow him, and Hayyan al-Nabati, the leader of his native auxiliaries, prevented them from declaring support. He was killed at Ferghana by Arab soldiers, led by the Tamim tribe.

Most of his conquests were lost in the following years, and the Umayyads restored control of most of Transoxiana only after 738 under Nasr ibn Sayyar. The local princes accepted Muslim rule as final after the Abbasid victory at the Battle of Talas in 751. Pilgrims later venerated places in Ferghana said to hold his tomb.
qutb-minar: The Ghurids, a clan from Ghur in what is now western Afghanistan, annexed Multan and Uch in 1175-76 and Sindh in 1185-86. In 1193 Qutb al-Din Aibak conquered Delhi. After the defeat of Prithviraj Chauhan, the last Hindu ruler of Delhi before the conquest, he began a victory tower to mark the start of Islamic rule in the region. It rose over the ruins of the Lal Kot, the citadel of Dhillika, after the neighbouring Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque. The Minaret of Jam in Afghanistan, of about 1190, is a decade or so older.

Aibak finished only the first storey. His successor and son-in-law Shamsuddin Iltutmish added three more. After lightning damaged the top, Firuz Shah Tughlaq replaced it, added another storey and a cupola. The name is usually taken from Aibak, though it may honour the Sufi saint Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki, to whom Iltutmish was devoted.

The tower is 72.5 metres high and tapers from a base 14.3 metres across to 2.7 metres at the top. Its fluted shaft has stalactite-like bracketing under the balconies, and bands of inscriptions in naskh script carry Quranic verses and the titles of the Ghurid rulers Ghiyath al-Din and Mu'izz al-Din. Hindu craftsmen worked under Muslim architects, and some inscriptions are disarranged Quranic passages, since the craftsmen did not know the text.

Beside it stands the Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque, begun by Aibak in 1199, the earliest surviving mosque built by the Delhi sultans. It was built with columns from 27 Jain and Hindu temples, as Aibak's own inscription records. In its courtyard stands an iron pillar with a Sanskrit inscription of the fourth century CE, set up as a standard of the god Vishnu.

An earthquake damaged the minaret in 1505 and Sikandar Lodi repaired it. In 1828 Major Robert Smith renovated it and added a cupola, which was taken down in 1848 and re-erected on the ground nearby as Smith's Folly. Scholars have called the tower the earliest and best example of a fusion of Hindu and Muslim traditions. The Qutb complex became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993. After a stampede on the dark staircase on 4 December 1981 killed 45 people, mostly schoolchildren, the tower was closed to the public.
qutb-ud-din-aibak: Aibak came from Turkestan and belonged to a Turkic tribe of the same name, a word derived from the Turkic terms for moon and lord. Separated from his family as a child, he was taken to the slave market of Nishapur, where a qazi, Fakhruddin Abdul Aziz Kufi, bought him. He was treated affectionately, educated with the qazi's sons and taught archery, horse-riding and Qur'an recital. He was resold to a merchant, who sold him to the Ghurid Sultan Muhammad Ghori at Ghazni. He rose to be Amir-i Akhur, officer of the royal stables, and after being captured by Khwarazmian scouts and held in an iron cage he was released and favoured by the Sultan.

Aibak served at the first and second battles of Tarain, and after the Ghurid victory of 1192 Muhammad Ghori placed him over the former Chahamana territory at Kuhram. He took Meerut, Baran and Delhi in 1192; in 1193 he deposed the Tomara ruler there and took direct control. He fought in the campaign against the Gahadavala king Jayachandra, defeated the Chaulukya army at Mount Abu in 1197 and plundered Anhilwara, and besieged Kalinjar in 1202. His campaigns involved the large-scale capture of slaves; Hasan Nizami gives 20,000 for Gujarat and 50,000 for Kalinjar, figures that Irfan Habib thinks exaggerated.

After Muhammad Ghori was assassinated in March 1206, the citizens of Lahore asked Aibak to take sovereign power, and he informally ascended the throne on 25 June 1206. He disputed Ghurid territory with his father-in-law Taj al-Din Yildiz and at one point took Ghazni. In 1208 to 1209 Ghiyasuddin Mahmud sent him a ceremonial parasol and a deed recognising him as ruler of Hindustan.

In 1210 Aibak fell from his horse while playing chaugan, a form of polo, at Lahore and died when the pommel of the saddle pierced his ribs. He left no named heir. Turkic officers appointed Aram Shah, who ruled no more than eight months before Iltutmish, Aibak's former slave and son-in-law, defeated him and made the loosely held territories into the Delhi Sultanate. The line is called the Mamluk or Slave dynasty, though only Aibak, Iltutmish and Balban were slaves.

Contemporary chroniclers praised his generosity, which earned him the epithet lakh-bakhsh. The Qutb Minar in Delhi was begun in his reign, and the Adhai Din Ka Jhonpra in Ajmer is also attributed to him. His tomb is in Anarkali Bazaar, Lahore.
qutuz: Sayf ad-Din Qutuz is said to have been a Khwarazmian prince of Turkic origin, captured by the Mongols during their conquest of the Khwarazmian Empire around 1231. Sources give his name as Mahmud ibn Mamdud and make him a nephew of Jalal al-Din and a grandson of Muhammad II of Khwarazm. He was taken to Damascus and sold to an Egyptian slave merchant, who sold him to the Mamluk sultan Aybak in Cairo. He became the most prominent Mu'izi Mamluk of Aybak and in 1253 his vice-sultan. In 1250 he had been a commander at the Battle of Mansurah against the Seventh Crusade.

Aybak was assassinated in 1257, and Qutuz remained vice-sultan to Aybak's son al-Mansur Ali, in effect ruling Egypt. In November 1257 and April 1258 he defeated raids from al-Malik al-Mughith of Al-Karak.

The Mongols sacked Baghdad in February 1258 and advanced into Syria. Qutuz told the emirs that Egypt needed a strong sultan, and on 12 November 1259 he deposed the 15-year-old al-Mansur Ali. When Hulagu sent a letter demanding submission, Qutuz had the messengers executed and their heads mounted on the Bab Zuweila gate of Cairo. He then led an army north instead of waiting for an attack. The Crusaders of Acre, whom the Mongols had also approached, stayed neutral but allowed his army to pass through their territory and to camp and resupply near Acre.

At the Battle of Ain Jalut on 3 September 1260, in south-eastern Galilee, the Mamluk army under Qutuz and Baybars met a Mongol force led by Kitbuqa. The Egyptian left flank was damaged at first, but Qutuz rallied his troops and the Mongols were defeated; Kitbuqa was killed. It was the first defeat the Mongols had suffered since attacking the Islamic world. The Mamluks then took Damascus and extended their rule over the Levant to the Euphrates.

On the way back to Cairo, Qutuz was assassinated on a hunting expedition at Salihiyah, on 24 October 1260. Muslim and Western historians alike hold that Baybars was involved, and medieval Mamluk chroniclers give his motives as the death of his friend Faris ad-Din Aktai or Qutuz's grant of Aleppo to another emir, whom he had promised to Baybars. Baybars returned to Cairo and became sultan. Qutuz was buried first at Al-Qusair and later in a cemetery in Cairo.

His reign lasted less than a year, but he is remembered as one of the most popular Mamluk sultans and holds the honorific the Lion of Ain Jalut. Hulagu was soon occupied by the war with the Golden Horde and died in 1265 without avenging the defeat.
